questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
Access to affordable credit remains one of the biggest obstacles facing small business owners across many developing economies. Traditional banks are often reluctant to lend to fledgling enterprises that lack collateral or a lengthy credit history, leaving many entrepreneurs to depend on personal savings or informal moneylenders who typically charge exorbitant interest rates. In response, microfinance institutions have emerged, offering smaller loans with more flexible requirements to those excluded from conventional banking. Advocates insist that this model has empowered countless traders and artisans to expand their businesses and lift their households out of poverty. Critics, however, warn that some microfinance schemes still impose steep interest rates and rigid repayment schedules that can trap borrowers in cycles of debt rather than freeing them from hardship. Until lending practices are more closely regulated, the true impact of microfinance on small business growth will remain a subject of debate.

According to the passage, why are traditional banks often reluctant to lend to small business owners?
options: They refuse to work with entrepreneurs entirely
They lack collateral or a lengthy credit history
They only lend to informal moneylenders
They already have too much money saved
questions.explanation: The passage states banks are 'reluctant to lend to fledgling enterprises that lack collateral or a lengthy credit history.'

What is the closest meaning of the word 'exorbitant' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Exorbitant' describes something (often a price or rate) that is unreasonably or excessively high.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Neither the manager nor the staff ___ aware of the new policy.'
questions.explanation: When 'neither...nor' joins a singular and plural subject, the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'staff' (plural here) takes 'were'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The lecturer's argument was remarkably COGENT.'
questions.explanation: 'Cogent' means clear, logical, and convincing, making 'convincing' the closest synonym.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The two politicians remained BELLIGERENT throughout the debate.'
questions.explanation: 'Belligerent' means hostile and aggressive; its opposite is 'peaceful.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Bureaucracy' is correctly spelt with 'eau' following the 'r'; the other options misspell the word.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'If I ___ known about the exam earlier, I would have prepared better.'
questions.explanation: This is a third conditional describing an unreal past scenario, requiring the past perfect: 'if I had known.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct preposition to complete the sentence: 'The results were consistent ___ our expectations.'
questions.explanation: 'Consistent with' is the standard prepositional pairing meaning in agreement with something.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word: 'The QUIETLY spoken man surprised everyone with his wit.'
questions.explanation: 'Quietly' modifies 'spoken', describing how it was done, making it an adverb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that is the correct plural form of 'criterion'.
questions.explanation: 'Criterion', of Greek origin, forms its plural irregularly as 'criteria'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The new intern had to LEARN THE ROPES quickly.'
options: Learn the basic skills of a job
questions.explanation: 'Learn the ropes' is an idiom meaning to learn the basic tasks or skills required for a job.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'Mathematics ___ considered a difficult subject by many students.'
questions.explanation: Although 'mathematics' ends in 's', it functions as a singular subject when naming the discipline, requiring 'is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: 'Her ___ comments during the review hurt her colleague's feelings.'
questions.explanation: 'Callous' means insensitive to the feelings of others, fitting the context of hurtful comments.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
options: We need three items: bread, milk, and eggs.
We need three items; bread, milk, and eggs.
We need three items, bread milk and eggs.
We need three items bread, milk, and eggs.
questions.explanation: A colon correctly introduces the list following the complete independent clause, with commas separating list items.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The jury ___ still deliberating when the recess was called.'
questions.explanation: 'Jury' is typically treated as a singular collective noun in this context, taking the singular verb 'was'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech used: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'
questions.explanation: Giving the wind the human ability to 'whisper' is an example of personification.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The company's expansion plans were rather AMBITIOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Ambitious' describes plans that are bold and aspire to significant achievement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct form of the verb: 'Each of the candidates ___ given a fair chance to speak.'
questions.explanation: 'Each' is grammatically singular, so it takes the singular verb 'was', regardless of the plural noun that follows.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'This is the laboratory ___ equipment was recently upgraded.'
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun correctly linking 'the laboratory' to 'its equipment.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The professor's explanation was surprisingly SUCCINCT.'
questions.explanation: 'Succinct' means expressed briefly and clearly; its opposite is 'verbose', meaning wordy.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: 'She had barely sat down ___ the phone rang.'
questions.explanation: 'Had barely...when' is the standard construction linking two closely sequential past events.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: 'Occurrence' is correctly spelt with double 'c' and double 'r'; the other options are misspellings.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'It was they who ___ chosen to represent the class.'
questions.explanation: The subject 'they' requires the plural verb 'were' for grammatical agreement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The manager gave a rather TERSE reply to the question.'
questions.explanation: 'Terse' means using few words, often in a blunt or abrupt manner, making 'curt and brief' the best synonym.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'Between you and ___, I think the plan will fail.'
questions.explanation: After the preposition 'between', the objective case pronoun 'me' is correct, not the subjective 'I'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'The number of applicants ___ increased significantly this year.'
questions.explanation: 'The number of' (referring to a specific total) takes a singular verb, unlike 'a number of', which takes a plural verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the sentence: 'The manager decided to turn a blind eye to the minor infractions.'
options: He literally could not see the infractions
questions.explanation: 'Turn a blind eye' is an idiom meaning to deliberately ignore something one does not wish to acknowledge.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The ancient artefact was remarkably well PRESERVED.'
options: Kept intact and protected from damage
questions.explanation: 'Preserved' means kept in its original state and protected from decay or damage.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Everyone must submit they assignment by Friday.
Everyone must submit his or her assignment by Friday.
Everyone must submit our assignment by Friday.
Everyone must submit their assignment by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is grammatically singular, so in traditional formal usage it correctly pairs with the singular possessive 'his or her.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The politician's speech was full of PLATITUDES.'
questions.explanation: 'Platitude' means a trite, overused remark lacking original thought.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The witness gave a very CANDID account of events.'
questions.explanation: 'Candid' means open and honest; its opposite is 'deceptive.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The old bridge was considered quite PRECARIOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Precarious' means unstable or likely to fail or collapse.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'His decision to resign was entirely VOLUNTARY.'
questions.explanation: 'Voluntary' means done by choice; its opposite is 'compulsory,' meaning required.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The teacher's explanation was so LUCID that everyone understood.'
questions.explanation: 'Lucid' means expressed clearly and easy to understand.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The manager remained IMPASSIVE despite the bad news.'
questions.explanation: 'Impassive' means showing no emotion; its opposite is 'emotional.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The new evidence CORROBORATED the witness's story.'
questions.explanation: 'Corroborate' means to confirm or support a statement with evidence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The professor's tone was surprisingly BENEVOLENT.'
questions.explanation: 'Benevolent' means kind and well-meaning; its opposite is 'malicious.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The company's profits showed a GRADUAL increase over the year.'
questions.explanation: 'Gradual' describes something that happens slowly and steadily over time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The suspect's alibi was found to be SPURIOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Spurious' means false or not genuine; its opposite is 'genuine.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'She made a FRIVOLOUS complaint about the noise.'
questions.explanation: 'Frivolous' means lacking seriousness or importance.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The old man was known for his FRUGAL lifestyle.'
questions.explanation: 'Frugal' means economical or sparing; its opposite is 'extravagant,' meaning wasteful with money.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The negotiations reached an AMICABLE settlement.'
questions.explanation: 'Amicable' means characterised by friendliness and absence of discord.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'His argument was quite DUBIOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Dubious' means doubtful or uncertain; its opposite is 'certain.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The soldiers showed great TENACITY under pressure.'
questions.explanation: 'Tenacity' means firmness of purpose or persistence in the face of difficulty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The new employee was remarkably DILIGENT.'
questions.explanation: 'Diligent' means showing care and effort; its opposite is 'lazy.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The chairman's remarks were considered rather TACTLESS.'
questions.explanation: 'Tactless' means lacking sensitivity in dealing with others or with delicate situations.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The results of the experiment were AMBIGUOUS.'
questions.explanation: 'Ambiguous' means open to more than one interpretation, i.e. unclear; its opposite is 'clear.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the underlined word: 'The refugees were given TEMPORARY shelter.'
questions.explanation: 'Temporary' means lasting for only a limited time, i.e. short-term.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word opposite in meaning to the underlined word: 'The old law was considered OBSOLETE.'
questions.explanation: 'Obsolete' means no longer in use or out of date; its opposite is 'current.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'By the time we arrived, the movie ___ already started.'
questions.explanation: The past perfect 'had started' is needed to show an action completed before another past action (our arrival).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'She is one of the students who ___ always punctual.'
questions.explanation: 'Who' refers to 'students' (plural), so the verb must agree in the plural: 'are'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: '___ of the two candidates is more qualified for the job.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is used to refer to two items or persons when negating both; 'none' is used for three or more.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'He is not only intelligent ___ also hardworking.'
questions.explanation: 'Not only...but also' is a standard correlative conjunction pair.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'The committee ___ divided in their opinions on the matter.'
questions.explanation: When a collective noun's members act individually (divided opinions), the plural verb 'were' is used.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'I would rather you ___ me the truth from the start.'
questions.explanation: 'Would rather' followed by a subject requires the past subjunctive form: 'told'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'Hardly ___ the lecture begun when the fire alarm rang.'
questions.explanation: 'Hardly...when' requires the past perfect 'had begun' for the earlier of two past actions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'This is the same book ___ I lost last year.'
questions.explanation: After 'the same', the relative pronoun 'that' is the conventional choice, not 'what'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'Not one of the applicants ___ the required qualifications.'
questions.explanation: 'Not one of' takes a singular verb, since 'one' is the true subject.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'She acted as if she ___ the answer all along.'
questions.explanation: 'As if' introducing an unreal or hypothetical situation in the present typically uses the past subjunctive 'knew'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'The news of his promotion ___ everyone happy.'
questions.explanation: 'News' is singular in this context and the sentence is in the past tense, so 'made' is correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'Scarcely had the plane landed ___ passengers began to disembark.'
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely...when' is the standard correlative construction, similar to 'hardly...when'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: '___ you study hard, you will not pass the examination.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not', fitting the negative conditional sense of the sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'I look forward ___ from you soon.'
questions.explanation: 'Look forward to' is followed by a gerund, since 'to' functions here as a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'He denied ___ the missing documents.'
questions.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund ('denied taking'), not an infinitive.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'The teacher, along with her students, ___ attending the seminar.'
questions.explanation: Phrases introduced by 'along with' do not affect subject-verb agreement; the singular subject 'teacher' takes 'is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'No sooner had he sat down ___ the telephone rang.'
questions.explanation: 'No sooner...than' is the fixed correlative pairing used for closely sequential past actions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: '___ hard she tried, she could not solve the puzzle.'
questions.explanation: 'However' plus an adjective or adverb ('however hard') introduces a concessive clause meaning 'no matter how'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the correct option: 'The findings of the study ___ published next month.'
questions.explanation: 'Findings' is plural, and the passive future tense 'will be published' fits the context.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: 'He is used to ___ up early every morning.'
questions.explanation: 'Used to' (meaning accustomed to) is followed by a gerund: 'waking up'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'Her smile was as bright as the morning sun.'
questions.explanation: A simile compares two unlike things using 'as' or 'like'; here 'as bright as' signals a simile.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'Time is a thief that steals our youth.'
questions.explanation: A metaphor directly states that one thing IS another without using 'like' or 'as', as in calling time 'a thief'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'The classroom was as silent as a graveyard.'
questions.explanation: The comparison using 'as...as' between the classroom and a graveyard is a simile.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'I have told you a million times to clean your room.'
questions.explanation: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for emphasis; 'a million times' is clearly exaggerated.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.'
questions.explanation: The repetition of the initial 'p' sound across the words is alliteration.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'The bees buzzed lazily in the warm afternoon.'
questions.explanation: 'Buzzed' imitates the actual sound made by bees, which is onomatopoeia.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'The White House announced new policies today.'
questions.explanation: Metonymy substitutes a related term ('The White House') for what it represents (the US President or administration).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'The stars danced playfully in the night sky.'
questions.explanation: Giving stars the human ability to 'dance' attributes human qualities to a non-human thing, which is personification.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'It's raining cats and dogs outside.'
questions.explanation: 'Raining cats and dogs' is a fixed idiomatic, exaggerated expression meaning it is raining very heavily.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Identify the figure of speech: 'The crown will pass to the next heir in line.'
questions.explanation: 'The crown' stands for royal authority or the monarchy itself, a classic example of metonymy.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The manager decided to BITE THE BULLET and lay off some staff.'
options: Face a difficult situation with courage
questions.explanation: 'Bite the bullet' means to bravely endure a painful or unpleasant situation that is unavoidable.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'After the argument, the two friends decided to BURY THE HATCHET.'
options: Make peace and end their conflict
questions.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' means to make peace and stop arguing or fighting.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'He always wants to HAVE HIS CAKE AND EAT IT TOO.'
options: Wants the benefits of two conflicting choices at once
questions.explanation: This idiom describes wanting to enjoy two incompatible things at the same time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the proverb: 'A stitch in time saves nine.'
options: Timely action prevents bigger problems later
It is better to delay than to act
questions.explanation: This proverb teaches that dealing with a problem promptly saves more effort or trouble later.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the proverb: 'Do not count your chickens before they hatch.'
options: Do not assume success before it actually happens
Count everything carefully before selling it
Always plan far ahead of time
questions.explanation: This proverb warns against relying on something uncertain before it is actually confirmed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'She let the CAT OUT OF THE BAG during the party.'
options: Brought a pet to the party
questions.explanation: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret, often unintentionally.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the proverb: 'Too many cooks spoil the broth.'
options: Chefs should always work in teams
Having too many people involved can ruin a task
Broth is difficult to prepare well
questions.explanation: This proverb means that when too many people try to manage the same task, the result often suffers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The new policy was just WINDOW DRESSING and changed nothing important.'
options: A superficial or misleading appearance of improvement
questions.explanation: 'Window dressing' refers to something done merely to create a good but false impression.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the proverb: 'He who laughs last, laughs best.'
options: It is rude to laugh at others
Final success matters more than early confidence or mockery
Laughing is good for one's health
The first person to succeed always wins
questions.explanation: This proverb suggests ultimate triumph is more meaningful than an early advantage or premature celebration.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the idiom: 'The company decided to GO BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD after the product failed.'
options: Start planning again from the beginning
questions.explanation: 'Go back to the drawing board' means to restart a plan or process after a failed attempt.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word in which the letters 'ch' are pronounced differently from the others.
questions.explanation: In 'chef', 'ch' is pronounced /sh/ as in 'shoe', while in the other options it is pronounced /ch/ as in 'chin'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which of the following words has its main stress on the FIRST syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Photograph' is stressed on the first syllable (PHO-to-graph), unlike its derivatives, which shift the stress.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that does NOT rhyme with the others.
questions.explanation: 'Cough' is pronounced with an /off/ sound, while 'rough', 'tough', and 'enough' all end with the /uff/ sound.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that contains a silent letter.
questions.explanation: 'Knee' contains a silent 'k' before 'n', unlike the other words listed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: In which of the following words is the letter 'C' pronounced as /s/?
questions.explanation: Before 'i', 'e', or 'y', the letter 'c' is typically pronounced /s/, as in 'city'; before 'a', 'u', or 'o' it is usually pronounced /k/.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which of the following words carries its main stress on the SECOND syllable?
questions.explanation: As a verb, 'record' is stressed on the second syllable (re-CORD), while as a noun it is stressed on the first (RE-cord).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word whose vowel sound differs from the others.
questions.explanation: 'Blood' is pronounced with a short vowel sound, while 'food', 'mood', and 'moon' all have the long /oo/ sound.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word that rhymes with 'THROUGH'.
questions.explanation: 'Through' rhymes with 'blue', since both share the same long /oo/ vowel sound; the other options have different vowel sounds.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Which of the following words has a silent 'b'?
questions.explanation: In 'comb', 'bomb', and 'tomb', the final 'b' following 'm' is silent in each case.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: Choose the word with the main stress on the first syllable.
questions.explanation: 'Table' is a two-syllable word stressed on the first syllable, unlike the other options, which are stressed on the second syllable.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text: In which of the following words is the letter 'S' pronounced as /z/?

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
In recent years, many Nigerian households have turned to solar power as a reliable alternative to the epileptic electricity supplied by the national grid. Unlike petrol or diesel generators, which many families still rely on daily, solar panels produce no fumes and require little maintenance once properly installed. The major obstacle, however, remains the high upfront cost of purchasing panels, batteries, and inverters, which places the technology beyond the reach of many low-income households. Government incentives and falling equipment prices in recent years have begun to narrow this gap, and some rural communities now enjoy their first stable electricity supply through mini solar grids funded by non-governmental organisations. Even so, experts caution that without proper battery storage, solar power alone cannot fully replace the grid or generators, particularly for businesses that need electricity around the clock, including at night and during long stretches of cloudy weather.

According to the passage, what is one advantage of solar panels over generators?
options: They are provided free by the government
They are cheaper to purchase upfront
They work perfectly even without batteries at night
They produce no fumes and require little maintenance
questions.explanation: The passage states that 'unlike petrol or diesel generators...solar panels produce no fumes and require little maintenance.'

questions.subject: English Language
questions.text:
When Ada first walked into the university library as a fresh undergraduate, she was overwhelmed by the sheer number of shelves stretching from floor to ceiling. Having attended a secondary school with only a small reading room, she had never imagined that a single building could hold so many books. Within her first month, she discovered a quiet corner near a window overlooking the campus garden, and it soon became her favourite spot to study. Over time, Ada learned that success in her demanding engineering programme depended less on innate talent and more on consistent, disciplined effort. She began arriving at the library an hour before her first class each day, a habit her classmates found puzzling at first but later tried to imitate once they saw her grades improve. By her final year, Ada had not only mastered her coursework but had also become the student many others turned to for help understanding difficult concepts.

Why was Ada overwhelmed when she first entered the university library?
options: The library was too noisy for her to study
She could not find any books she needed
She was told she could not borrow any books
She had never seen so many books in one building before
questions.explanation: The passage explains she 'had never imagined that a single building could hold so many books,' having come from a school with only a small reading room.
